title: Surjective good diagrams and their fibre-product composition
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring. Call an integer cochain complex good if it is zero outside degrees $-1,0$ and its two terms are direct summands of finite free $A$-modules [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces isomorphisms on all $H^i=\ker(d^i)/\operatorname{im}(d^{i-1})$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]; a homotopy $f\simeq g$ means $f-g=dh+hd$ with $h$ of degree $-1$. Every quasi-isomorphism $a:P\to Q$ between good complexes has a good diagram $P\xleftarrow{b}M\xrightarrow{c}Q$, meaning that $b,c$ are degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphisms and $c\simeq ab$. More specifically, for every finite free surjection $p:F\to Q^{-1}$, such a diagram is given by $M=[P^{-1}\oplus F\xrightarrow{d_P\oplus1}P^0\oplus F]$, $b$ the projection, $c^{-1}(x,f)=a^{-1}(x)+p(f)$, and $c^0(x,f)=a^0(x)+d_Qp(f)$. Moreover, for degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphisms $u:M\to Q$ and $v:N\to Q$ between good complexes, their termwise fibre product $M\times_QN$ is good and both projections are degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphisms. Consequently diagrams for $a:P\to Q$ and $a':Q\to R$ compose by this fibre product to a good diagram for $a'a$.

source.place: Tag 0FJM (lemma-determinant-two-term-complexes), existence of good diagrams and the fibre product M_123 in the composition paragraph.

proof.text: Choose a finite free surjection $p:F\to Q^{-1}$: the projection from a finite free module having $Q^{-1}$ as a direct summand does this. Fix any such $p$. In each degree, $P^i\oplus F$ is a direct summand of a finite free module: take the direct sum of the given inclusion and retraction for $P^i$ with the identity of $F$. Thus the displayed $M$, with $d_M(x,f)=(d_Px,f)$, is good. The projection $b$ is a surjective chain map. Its cycles in degree $-1$ are exactly $(x,0)$ with $d_Px=0$, and $\operatorname{im}(d_M)=\operatorname{im}(d_P)\oplus F$. Hence $H^{-1}(b)$ and $H^0(b)$ are isomorphisms; all other cohomology groups vanish.

proof.text: The prescribed $c$ is a chain map since $d_Q(a^{-1}x+p(f))=a^0d_Px+d_Qp(f)=c^0d_M(x,f)$. Define $h^0:M^0\to Q^{-1}$ by $h^0(x,f)=p(f)$, with all other components zero. In degree $-1$, $(c-ab)^{-1}(x,f)=p(f)=h^0d_M(x,f)$; in degree $0$, $(c-ab)^0(x,f)=d_Qp(f)=d_Qh^0(x,f)$. Thus $c-ab=dh+hd$. The cited homotopy-invariance statement gives $H^i(c)=H^i(a)H^i(b)$, an isomorphism. Therefore $c$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

proof.text: The map $c^{-1}$ is surjective because $p$ is. For any $y\in Q^0$, surjectivity of $H^0(a)$ supplies $x\in P^0$ and $z\in Q^{-1}$ with $y=a^0x+d_Qz$. Choose $f\in F$ with $p(f)=z$; then $c^0(x,f)=y$. Outside these two degrees the target is zero. Consequently both legs are degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphisms and the homotopy in step 2 makes this a good diagram for $a$.

proof.text: For the given $u:M\to Q$, $v:N\to Q$, put $B^i=\{(m,n)\in M^i\oplus N^i\mid u^im=v^in\}$ with differential $(d_M,d_N)$; the chain-map equations show that it preserves this submodule. Both projections are surjective, by surjectivity of the opposite leg. Since $Q^i$ is projective, the cited splitting statement gives a section $s_i$ of $v^i$ and a retraction $N^i\to\ker(v^i)$. Thus $\ker(v^i)$ is a direct summand of $N^i$, hence of a finite free module by composing the inclusions and retractions. The mutually inverse maps $(m,k)\mapsto(m,s_i(u^im)+k)$ and $(m,n)\mapsto(m,n-s_i(u^im))$ identify $B^i$ with $M^i\oplus\ker(v^i)$, again a direct summand of a finite free module. Hence $B$ is good.

source.place: Tag 0FJM (lemma-determinant-two-term-complexes), proof: existence of good diagrams and fibre-product composition; elementwise details supplied here.

proof.text: Write $K^{-1}=\ker(v^{-1})$, $K^0=\ker(v^0)$. The restricted differential $d_K:K^{-1}\to K^0$ is injective: a cycle in its kernel is a degree $-1$ cohomology class killed by the injective $H^{-1}(v)$, and there are no degree $-1$ boundaries. For $k\in K^0$, injectivity of $H^0(v)$ gives $n\in N^{-1}$ with $d_Nn=k$. Now $v^{-1}n$ is a cycle of $Q$; surjectivity of $H^{-1}(v)$ gives a cycle $z\in N^{-1}$ with $v^{-1}z=v^{-1}n$ (again there are no boundaries in degree $-1$). Therefore $n-z\in K^{-1}$ maps to $k$. This proves that $d_K$ is bijective.

source.place: Tag 0FJM (lemma-determinant-two-term-complexes), proof: existence of good diagrams and fibre-product composition; elementwise details supplied here.

proof.text: For $\pi_M:B\to M$, every cycle $m\in M^{-1}$ has a lift $(m,n)\in B^{-1}$. Its differential is $(0,d_Nn)$ with $d_Nn\in K^0$. By step 5 subtract $(0,k)$ with $d_Kk=d_Nn$, obtaining a cycle lifting $m$. A cycle in the kernel of this projection is $(0,k)$ with $d_Kk=0$, hence zero; this proves bijectivity on $H^{-1}$. On $H^0$, surjectivity follows from surjectivity of $\pi_M^0$. If $(m,n)\in B^0$ maps to a boundary $m=d_Mm'$, lift $m'$ to $(m',n')\in B^{-1}$. Subtraction of its differential leaves $(0,n-d_Nn')$ in $K^0$, which is a boundary by step 5. Thus $H^0(\pi_M)$ is injective too. All other degrees vanish. Interchanging $(M,u)$ and $(N,v)$ in steps 5 and 6 proves the same for $\pi_N$.

proof.text:
Write the two diagrams as $(b_{12},c_{12})$ and $(b_{23},c_{23})$, and choose homotopies $c_{12}-ab_{12}=dh+hd$, $c_{23}-a'b_{23}=dh'+h'd$. Form $B=M_{12}\times_QM_{23}$ using $c_{12}$ and $b_{23}$. Steps 4--6 apply and $c_{12}\pi_{12}=b_{23}\pi_{23}$. Its outer legs $b_{12}\pi_{12}$ and $c_{23}\pi_{23}$ are surjective; their cohomology maps are composites of isomorphisms, so they are quasi-isomorphisms. Finally, with $H=h'\pi_{23}+a'h\pi_{12}$, the chain-map equations give
$$c_{23}\pi_{23}-a'ab_{12}\pi_{12}=(c_{23}-a'b_{23})\pi_{23}+a'(c_{12}-ab_{12})\pi_{12}=dH+Hd.$$
This is the required good diagram for $a'a$.
